_doc: Labelled derivability pairs for validating wiki.derivability_review.ModelDerivabilityJudge. Each case: a restricted SYNTHESIS + its SURVIVING sources (the GDPR-erased one removed) + ground-truth `derivable` (is the synthesis still fully supported by the surviving sources alone?). ASYMMETRIC by design: this is a GDPR fail-safe tool, so PRECISION on the 'derivable' class is the safety guard (the judge must NOT wrongly say derivable=true and suggest unrestricting content that leaned on the erased source), while recall is only a convenience (a missed-derivable page stays restricted until a human reviews it — the deterministic surviving-source floor already flags it as a candidate). Hence a HIGH precision floor and a LOOSE recall floor. Measured (2026-07-25, local model): precision 1.00, recall 0.67 (the one miss was a defensible conservative read of a generalizing paraphrase).

cases.synthesis: The service signs JWTs with RS256.
surviving: We chose RS256 for JWT signing so the public key verifies without sharing the secret.
The RS256 decision was recorded in the auth ADR.

cases.synthesis: Memory is stored locally in SQLite by default.
surviving: By default, memory lives in a local SQLite file on the user's hardware.
No cloud egress occurs in the default configuration.

cases.synthesis: Full-text search on PostgreSQL uses a tsvector column with a GIN index.
surviving: On PostgreSQL, files_search uses a generated tsvector column indexed with GIN, queried via @@ to_tsquery.

cases.synthesis: Access tokens expire after 15 minutes and refresh tokens after 30 days.
surviving: We chose RS256 for JWT signing.

cases.synthesis: Retrieval hits the correct session as the #1 result about 92% of the time.
surviving: Hybrid FTS+vector search with RRF is used for retrieval.

cases.synthesis: The Q3 incident was caused by a misconfigured connection pool.
surviving: The team uses PostgreSQL with a pooled connection layer.
